excerpt: Six keyboard shortcuts that replace hundreds of mouse movements, why they save your hands, and how to take a break before the ache turns into an injury.

body.text: This lesson teaches six keyboard shortcuts that save your hands, then shows you how to rest them. You will learn save, undo, find, copy, paste, and switch, and you will learn the break that keeps your wrists comfortable. Each shortcut replaces a journey with a mouse.
A shortcut is two or three keys pressed together. The computer does the same thing as the menu, in a fraction of the movement, and the saving adds up over a working day.
Before you start

items: Any laptop or desktop with a keyboard.
A document you are happy to experiment in.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: The six that matter most

items: Ctrl and S saves. In some programs it copies a version with a new name.
Ctrl and Z undoes the last thing, and works in almost every program.
Ctrl and C copies the selected text or file.
Ctrl and V pastes it where the cursor is.
Ctrl and F opens a search box for finding a word on the page.
Alt and Tab switches between open windows without the mouse.

body.text: You will see nothing visible happen for most of these, which is why they feel strange at first. The proof is in the result: the file saves, the mistake disappears, the window changes.

body.alt: Hands on a keyboard with the Ctrl and S keys pressed together.
body.caption: Ctrl and S, pressed together. Four hundred saves a year, and each one costs a fraction of a second.

body.text: It looks like shortcuts are for people who type quickly. They are for anybody whose wrist aches after an hour with a mouse, which is most people after a week.
Why they spare your hands

items: Every mouse trip moves your hand off the keyboard and back again.
A shortcut keeps the hand still and uses a finger you already have there.
Ctrl and F beats scrolling through twelve pages looking for one name.
Alt and Tab beats hunting for an icon behind another window.
Ctrl and Z means a mistake costs one second instead of a rewrite.
Saved work means a power cut costs nothing, which is the largest saving of all.

body.text: None of this needs new equipment. The same keyboard does the work with less movement, and the habit takes about a week to settle.

body.alt: A browser window with the find box open and a word highlighted.
body.caption: Ctrl and F opens a search box on the page. Type a word and the page jumps to it, which beats scrolling.

body.text: Then rest
Shortcuts reduce strain. They do not remove it. The other half of the lesson is the break, which is the part people skip.

items: Every twenty minutes, look across the room for twenty seconds.
Every hour, stand up and let your arms hang loose for a minute.
Keep your wrists straight, not bent up towards the screen.
Rest your forearms on the desk rather than holding them in the air.
Put the screen at eye level, or raise the laptop on a stack of books.
If your fingers tingle or go numb, stop and rest, then see a clinic if it continues.

body.text: Do not worry about losing working time to breaks. A minute every hour keeps the last hour as sharp as the first, and the ache that would have ended the day early never arrives.
The Mac versions
On a Mac, most of these use Command instead of Ctrl, with the same letters. The pattern travels, so the effort is small.

items: Command and S saves, and Command and Z undoes.
Command and C, then Command and V, copy and paste.
Command and F searches the page.
Command and Tab switches applications.
Command and Space opens a search for any file or program.
The key with the four loops is the Command key.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is harmless, and the first is the most common when you are learning.

items: The wrong window closes: Ctrl and Z does not reopen it. Use the browser's reopen-tab option.
Text disappears after a paste: undo with Ctrl and Z and check where the cursor was.
Ctrl and S does nothing in a browser: that page is not a document you can save.
The shortcut types a letter instead: Ctrl is not held. Hold it down first.
Copy and paste stops working: something else is on the clipboard, so select again.
Your hand still aches: the break matters more than the shortcut. Adjust the desk height.

body.text: Practice
Learn two shortcuts a day, which is enough.

items: Open a document, type a sentence, and save with Ctrl and S.
Delete the sentence and bring it back with Ctrl and Z.
Copy one word twice with Ctrl and C, then Ctrl and V.
Search for a word on a long page with Ctrl and F.
Switch between two windows with Alt and Tab, then stand up for a minute.

body.text: You now work with fewer movements and rest before the ache. In the next lesson you will use the phone keyboard, which has more hidden keys than it seems.

excerpt: Where the numbers and symbols hide on a phone keyboard, how to move the cursor precisely, and how to turn off the autocorrect that keeps changing names.

body.text: This lesson explains the keyboard on a phone: where the numbers and symbols hide, how to move the cursor, and how to stop autocorrect from changing names. You will type faster and fix fewer mistakes afterwards.
A phone keyboard uses one screen for three sets of characters. Learning where the hidden layers sit is the whole skill, and it takes ten minutes.
Before you start

items: A phone with any messaging or notes app open.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Find the numbers and symbols

items: Tap the key marked 123 to reach numbers and the common symbols.
Look for a key marked =< to reach brackets, currency, and maths signs.
Long press a letter to reach its accented version, such as é or ñ.
Long press a full stop to reach a comma, a question mark, and an exclamation mark.
Long press a number to reach a fraction or a related symbol.
Tap ABC or the calendar key to return to letters.

body.text: You will see the whole keyboard change layout when you tap 123, and change back when you tap ABC. Nothing is lost, because the text stays in the box.

body.alt: Two thumbs typing on a phone keyboard.
body.caption: The 123 key opens the number layer. Long pressing a letter opens accents, which is where names with accents live.

body.text: It looks like a phone keyboard has no way to type an apostrophe or a naira sign. Both sit one layer down, on the second symbols page.
Move the cursor without fighting it

items: Tap where you want the cursor, which usually lands close.
Then hold a finger on the space bar and slide, which moves the cursor letter by letter.
Double tap a word to select it.
Hold on a word to select it and open the menu for copy and paste.
Use the handles on the selection to widen it to a whole sentence.
Tap the small arrow on the suggestion bar to undo an autocorrect.

body.text: A small magnified view appears above your finger while you slide on the space bar, which shows exactly where the cursor will land. Let go and it settles there.
The selection handles will appear as two small blue markers at each end of the word. Drag either one and the highlighted area grows, with a menu of copy, cut, and paste opening above it.

body.alt: A phone keyboard with a long press on a key showing extra symbols.
body.caption: Long press any key and its extra characters appear above it. Slide to the one you want and release.

body.text: Autocorrect, and how to live with it
Autocorrect guesses the word you meant. It is helpful in ordinary sentences and destructive with names, local words, and account numbers.

items: Watch the suggestion bar above the keyboard, which offers three guesses.
Tap the correct suggestion rather than typing the whole word.
If a name is changed, tap the word and choose the original from the suggestions.
Add important names to the keyboard dictionary so it stops correcting them.
For account numbers and codes, switch autocorrect off for that field if the phone allows.
Turn predictive text off completely in settings if it interferes more than it helps.

body.text: None of this needs a new keyboard app. The one already installed has every setting under Language and input in the phone's settings.
Do not worry about a message with one wrong word. Everybody who reads a phone message understands a slip, and the meaning almost always survives.
Speed, without the errors

items: Use swipe typing if it is offered: slide between letters without lifting a finger.
Type in short sentences, which are easier to correct than long ones.
Press the microphone key when speaking is faster than typing.
Double tap the space bar for a full stop in most keyboards.
Use the enter key on a phone form, which often moves to the next field.
Read the message once before sending, since autocorrect hides in plain sight.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here is a setting or a tap, and none of them loses your text.

items: The keyboard has disappeared: tap the text box again, which brings it back.
Every word is underlined in red: the wrong language is set. Change it in keyboard settings.
The keyboard is too small: turn the phone sideways, or use the one-handed setting.
Your name is always changed: add it to the dictionary.
Numbers come out as symbols: the number row is on a different layout. Check the 123 key.
The keyboard types in another language: hold the space bar and choose the language.

body.text: Practice
Ten minutes of deliberate typing fixes years of small frustration.

items: Type your name, then long press it to see the accent options.
Find the naira sign on the second symbols page.
Move the cursor with the space bar and correct one letter.
Add a family name to the dictionary.
Send a short message and read it once before sending.

body.text: You can now type on glass without fighting it. In the next lesson you will speak to the keyboard and let it write for you.

excerpt: How to turn speech into text on a phone or laptop, what to say for punctuation, and how to check the result before you send it.

body.text: This lesson teaches voice typing: speaking and letting the device write the words. You will turn on the microphone, speak in a way it understands, add punctuation by voice, and check the result. It is the fastest way to write a long message on a small screen.
Voice typing sends your speech to a recognition service, which returns text. It works well in a quiet room and struggles near a generator, a market, or a loud fan.
Before you start

items: A phone or laptop with a microphone.
A place with as little background noise as you can find.
About ten minutes.

body.text: Turn it on

items: Open any app with a text box and tap into it.
Look for a small microphone on the keyboard, usually near the space bar.
Tap it once. The keyboard shows a listening screen with a moving wave.
Speak at a normal pace, not slowly and not loudly.
Tap the microphone again when you finish, or pause and it stops on its own.
Read the text before sending, since recognition makes small errors.

body.text: You will see the words appear as you speak, slightly behind your voice, with the microphone icon pulsing. Words you would normally spell appear as the recogniser hears them, in the spelling you set.

body.alt: A phone keyboard showing the microphone key and a listening indicator.
body.caption: The microphone sits on the keyboard itself. One tap starts it, and a second tap ends it.

body.text: It looks like voice typing needs an internet connection every time. Most phones now recognise speech on the device, so it often works with no data at all.
Speaking so it understands

items: Say the punctuation: full stop, comma, question mark, new line.
Speak in short sentences rather than one long breath.
Say numbers slowly, and read account numbers digit by digit.
Spell a name letter by letter if it keeps coming out wrong.
Say the word no if a wrong word appears, which removes it in some keyboards.
Keep the phone about a hand's width from your mouth.

body.text: A spoken comma appears as a punctuation mark rather than the word, which is the sign that the setting is working. If the word comma appears in the text, the keyboard is not set for commands.

body.alt: A laptop screen showing dictated text in a document.
body.caption: Dictation works in a word processor too. The same habit applies: speak in sentences, then read the result.

body.text: Check before you send
Recognition confuses words that sound alike, and the errors are usually small and visible.

items: Read the whole message, not the first line.
Check names, which are the most common error.
Check numbers, especially amounts and phone numbers.
Check that punctuation spoken aloud did not become a word.
Check the tone, since spoken words can read bluntly when written down.
Correct with the keyboard for anything important, such as a bank instruction.

body.text: None of this replaces your judgement. The device writes, and you decide whether the words say what you meant.
Do not worry about the odd wrong word. A message with one error is still a message sent, and the receiver reads the meaning rather than the spelling.
Where it saves the most time

items: A long message to family, which would take five minutes with thumbs.
Notes after a meeting, spoken while they are fresh.
Searching for something, since speaking a query is faster than typing it.
Writing a first draft, which you then correct by keyboard.
Filling a complaint form, where the wording matters and typing is slow.
A shopping list, spoken as you walk through the market.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a plain cause, and most are about the room.

items: Nothing appears when you speak: the microphone permission is denied for the keyboard.
The words are wrong from the start: background noise, or the wrong language set.
It stops after a few words: the app timed out. Tap the microphone again.
It writes in another language: change the dictation language in settings.
It hears your accent poorly: speak slightly more slowly and closer to the phone.
It refuses to work offline: that device needs a connection. Type instead, or move to data.

body.text: Practice
Dictate one paragraph and correct it, which teaches the whole skill.

items: Open a note and tap the microphone.
Dictate three sentences with punctuation spoken aloud.
Stop and read the result.
Correct one wrong word with the keyboard.
Send the corrected note to yourself.

body.text: You can now write without typing every letter. In the next lesson you will read and answer email on the phone, which is where most people actually meet it.

excerpt: Setting up email on a phone, reading and replying, attaching a photo or a scan, and the notification settings that stop the phone buzzing all day.

body.text: This lesson sets up email on a phone and shows you how to use it well. You will add the account, read and reply, attach a file from the phone, and quieten the notifications. Email on a phone is how most people answer an office before the office closes.
The phone email app is the same mailbox as the one on a computer. A message read on the phone is read everywhere, because the mail sits on the server rather than on either device.
Before you start

items: Your email address and password.
A phone with data or wifi.
About fifteen minutes.

body.text: Add the account

items: Open the Gmail app, or Settings then Accounts on an iPhone.
Choose Add account, then Google or Other, depending on your mail.
Type the full address, including the part after the @.
Type the password, watching capital letters.
Approve the sign-in on the screen that appears.
Choose whether to sync mail, contacts, and calendar, which are separate switches.

body.text: You will see the inbox fill with the most recent messages, and the account name appear at the top of the list. Older mail arrives over the next few minutes as the phone downloads it.

body.alt: A phone showing an email inbox with unread messages.
body.caption: The inbox looks the same as on a computer. What you read here shows as read there, because the mailbox lives on the server.

body.text: It looks like a phone email is a copy that can drift from the real one. It is the same mailbox, and any change shows up on every device within a minute.
Read, reply, and forward

items: Tap a message to open it, and read from the top.
Swipe the message list to archive, which removes it from the inbox without deleting.
Tap the reply arrow, which answers only the sender.
Choose reply all only when everyone needs the answer.
Forward when somebody else must handle it, and say why in one line.
Add a signature with your name and number, so the reply carries your details.

body.text: The reply screen will show the quoted message underneath, with your cursor above it. That position is deliberate, since your answer reads first and the history sits below.

body.alt: A phone email compose screen with an attach paperclip and a file list.
body.caption: The paperclip opens the phone's files and photos. Choose where the file lives, then wait for the attachment to finish.

body.text: Attach something from the phone

items: Tap the paperclip in the compose screen.
Choose Photos for an image, or Files for a document.
Find the file in the folder list, which mirrors the phone's storage.
Tap once to attach, and wait for the small circle to finish.
Send a PDF rather than ten photos when the receiver needs a document.
Check the size shown beside the attachment, and shrink large photos if needed.

body.text: None of these need a computer. A scan made on the phone, attached on the phone, and sent from the phone is accepted by most offices.
Do not worry about sending from a phone looking less professional. The message arrives in the same inbox with the same words.
Stop the buzzing

items: Open the app settings and turn notifications off for promotions first.
Set notifications for important senders only, which is a setting in most apps.
Turn off notifications for the whole app if you check mail at set times instead.
Keep the badge count off, which removes the red number on the icon.
Set the app to sync only on wifi if data is expensive.
Check the account every morning and every evening, which is enough for most work.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a fix, and the password is the most common cause.

items: The password is rejected: it may have been changed on a computer. Update it in the phone settings.
Mail will not load: data is off, or the account needs re-authentication. Open the app and approve it.
The attachment will not send: the file is too large. Shrink the photo or send a link.
Messages arrive late: sync is set to wifi only, or battery saver is restricting the app.
The phone shows an old inbox: pull down on the list to refresh.
You signed out by mistake: add the account again with the same steps.

body.text: Practice
One received message, one reply, one attachment.

items: Add the account and open the inbox.
Open one message and read the whole thread.
Reply to yourself with a single sentence.
Attach a photo and send it.
Turn off promotion notifications and check the phone is quieter.

body.text: You can now handle email wherever you are. In the next lesson you will choose a file to upload and watch it arrive on the other side.

excerpt: What the Choose file button actually does, how to find the document in your folders, why an upload stalls, and how to check it worked.

body.text: This lesson explains uploading: choosing a file on your device and sending it to a website. You will find the file in your folders, watch the upload finish, and check that the other side actually received it.
Uploading moves a copy of a file from your device to a service on the internet. The original stays where it is, so nothing is lost by uploading.
Before you start

items: A file you need to send, such as a CV or a scanned form.
A website or app that asks for one.
About ten minutes.

body.text: What the button does

items: Look for a button marked Choose file, Browse, or Upload.
Tap it, and a file picker opens showing your folders.
The picker starts in a default place, which is rarely where your file is.
Use the sidebar to reach Documents, Downloads, or Pictures.
Tap the file once to select it, then confirm.
The website now shows the file name beside the button.

body.text: You will see the file name appear next to the button, with a small icon for its type. That name appearing is the sign that the site has accepted your choice, before anything is sent.

body.alt: A web form with a Choose file button and a selected file name.
body.caption: The file name beside the button proves the choice. Nothing is uploaded until you press the submit or send button.

body.text: It looks like choosing the file has already sent it. Nothing leaves the device until you press the final button, which is why you can still change your mind.
Find the file when the picker is confusing

items: Recent or Last used often has the file at the top.
Downloads holds everything you saved from a browser.
Documents holds what you made in Word or Excel.
Pictures or Photos holds scans and screenshots.
On a phone, the picker may open a gallery instead of folders.
If you cannot find it, search the file name in the picker's search box.

body.text: A shortcut worth knowing: save the file to the Desktop first, which most pickers show as the first place. The fewer folders to remember, the faster the upload.
The picker will show each file with its name, size, and the date it was changed, which helps when two files share a name. A tick appears beside the one you chose, and the window closes by itself.

body.alt: A website showing an upload progress bar at completion.
body.caption: The bar fills from left to right. When it disappears and a tick appears, the copy has arrived.

body.text: What happens during an upload

items: A progress bar shows how much has gone, not how long is left.
A slow connection makes the bar crawl, which is normal rather than broken.
Do not close the tab while it is moving.
Keep the phone awake, since some uploads pause when the screen locks.
A large file on a weak signal may need the phone kept on and near a window.
Wait for a confirmation message before you switch off.

body.text: Do not worry if the bar seems stuck at ninety per cent. The last part is often the slowest, and the confirmation comes when it finishes.
Checking it worked

items: Look for a message saying Uploaded, Received, or Thank you.
Check your email for a confirmation, since most services send one.
If the site shows a list of your files, refresh and look for yours.
Download the file and open it, which is the only real proof.
Note the time and the file name, in case you must follow up.
If nothing confirms, ask the receiver before uploading again.

body.text: If it goes wrong
Every case here has a next step, and a slow connection is usually the cause.

items: The site rejects the file type: it wants a PDF. Convert or scan it as one.
The site says the file is too large: shrink the photo or split the document.
The upload fails at the end: the connection dropped. Try again on a stronger signal.
Nothing happens when you press choose: the browser blocked a pop-up. Allow it for that site.
The file uploads but the receiver cannot open it: check the format before sending again.
You uploaded the wrong file: most forms allow a replace before submitting, so check first.

body.text: Practice
Upload something harmless to a site you trust, and watch each stage.

items: Find a small file and note where it lives.
Use a site with an upload button and press it.
Navigate to the file and select it.
Read the file name beside the button before submitting.
Watch the bar to the end and look for the confirmation.

body.text: You can now move a file from your device to the world. In the next lesson you will keep the papers that matter where a bag cannot lose them.
